Castigate

KAS-ti-gate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To castigate to criticize or reprimand someone severely, especially in public.

The senator was castigated by the press for the leaked memo.

Worked Example

The newspaper's editorial castigated the mayor for months of broken promises, calling the administration a complete failure.

A harsh, public, formal condemnation in print is exactly the severe criticism castigate describes.

How Strong Is It? — criticize → castigate → excoriate

criticize vs. castigate

criticize vs. castigate: To criticize is a general, everyday act of pointing out faults; to castigate is a much harsher, often public condemnation.

excoriate vs. castigate

excoriate vs. castigate: Excoriate goes even further than castigate, implying an almost scathing, merciless verbal attack.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — cast

root — cast: pure (Latin (castus))

suffix — -igate

suffix — -igate: to make, to do (Latin (agere))

Put it together

Put it together: cast ('pure', from Latin castus) + -igate ('to make, to do') together trace back to the idea of correcting someone to make them 'pure' again -- the harsh, formal criticism castigate now describes.

Use the root in a new word: chaste

Use the root in a new word: chaste: Chaste comes from the same Latin root castus ('pure'), the same root buried inside castigate.
